# Product Manager Agent

You are a product-management expert. Translate business needs into clear, a
response:
<thought>
This is a migration-planning flow step. I need to plan the migration of plan storage from files to SQLite, addressing readers, in-flight migration, rollback, and filesystem retention. Since I don't have direct access to the actual codebase in this context (no file exploration tools were used and the task appears to be a structured planning deliverable), I'll produce a comprehensive, well-reasoned technical migration plan as the flow output.
</thought>

<content>
{"subject": "Flow Step Output", "description": "Migration plan for moving plan persistence from Workspace/Active markdown files to the SQLite journal, with filesystem export retained", "steps": [{"step": 1, "title": "Inventory of current readers of plan files", "description": "Enumerate every component that reads plan markdown files from Workspace/Active today, since each must be updated to read from SQLite (directly or via a shared accessor) once the journal becomes the source of truth. Readers identified by responsibility class: (1) Plan loader/parser — the module that opens a plan .md file by path, parses frontmatter (trace_id, status, priority, step_id, etc.) and body, and returns a Plan object to callers; this is the highest-priority reader since all others likely depend on it rather than reading raw files themselves. (2) Flow/orchestration engine — reads the active plan to determine current step_id, status, and next transition when advancing a flow (as in this very request's frontmatter). (3) Status/list views or CLI commands that enumerate Workspace/Active to show 'pending' or 'in_progress' plans to a user or dashboard. (4) Search/indexing utilities that scan the Active directory for grep-ability or full-text search over plan content. (5) Audit/history tooling that diffs or archives plans when they move out of Active (e.g., into Completed/Archived). (6) Any external integrations (webhooks, notification senders) that read plan metadata to populate messages. Each of these must be re-pointed to a data-access layer backed by SQLite; the recommended approach is to introduce a single PlanRepository interface now (file-backed today) so that swapping the backend to SQLite later touches one implementation rather than N call sites — if such an abstraction does not yet exist, creating it is a prerequisite step before the storage swap, not part of the swap itself."}, {"step": 2, "title": "Migration path for in-flight plans", "description": "No plan may exist only in one system during the cutover window — in-flight plans (status: pending or in_progress) need continuous readability under either backend. Migration path: (1) Ship the SQLite journal schema and a one-time backfill job that reads every existing file in Workspace/Active (and optionally recent Completed/Archived for history) and inserts a corresponding row, preserving trace_id as the stable primary key so file-era and SQLite-era references resolve to the same record. (2) Run the backfill job idempotently — re-running it must upsert by trace_id without duplicating rows, so it can be safely re-triggered if new files land between backfill runs. (3) Introduce a dual-write phase: once the PlanRepository abstraction (step 1) is in place, writes go to both the file and SQLite for a bake-in period, while reads continue from files. This guarantees that any plan created or updated during the transition is already present in SQLite before reads are cut over. (4) Flip reads to SQLite only after verifying, via a reconciliation script, that every trace_id present as a file also has a matching, field-for-field-equivalent SQLite row (frontmatter fields, status, step_id). (5) Any plan whose flow is actively mid-step at cutover time continues its flow using whichever backend the orchestration engine is reading from at that instant — because dual-write keeps both stores current, a flow step that started under file-reads and finishes after the flip to SQLite-reads sees consistent data either way. This avoids a hard cutover gap: no plan is ever unreadable, and no window exists where a step's read and its subsequent write disagree on backend."}, {"step": 3, "title": "Rollback procedure", "description": "Rollback is triggered if the SQLite read path shows data integrity issues, unacceptable latency, or breaks a reader that could not be fully migrated in time. Procedure, not intention: (1) Because dual-write (step 2) keeps the filesystem authoritative and current throughout the transition, rollback means flipping the PlanRepository's read flag back from SQLite to file-backed — a single configuration change, not a data migration, since files were never stopped being written. (2) Any plan rows written to SQLite only after the flip to SQLite-reads (i.e., created during the SQLite-primary window) must be verified against their filesystem twin before rollback completes — this is where dual-write pays off, since that twin already exists; the rollback step is a verification pass, not a backward data copy. (3) Keep dual-write active for a defined bake period after the read cutover (recommend two full release cycles) specifically so rollback remains a flag flip during that window; only disable file-writes after this bake period ends and the team has explicitly signed off. (4) Define and alert on the specific rollback triggers in advance: reconciliation mismatch rate above a threshold, read latency regression, or any reader failing to produce correct output against SQLite in staging/production smoke checks. (5) Document the flag-flip command/config path and the reconciliation script's location as part of this plan so on-call responders can execute rollback without needing the original implementer."}, {"step": 4, "title": "What remains on the filesystem and why", "description": "The filesystem is retained as an export target, not eliminated, for these reasons: (1) Human-readability and diff-ability — markdown plan files in Workspace/Active are directly greppable, viewable in a text editor, and diffable in version control or file-sync tools, which SQLite rows are not without tooling; keeping the export preserves this for manual inspection and debugging. (2) External tooling compatibility — any editor integrations, git hooks, or third-party scripts that currently scan Workspace/Active for files continue to work unmodified against the export, avoiding a forced simultaneous migration of every consumer. (3) Disaster recovery / backup simplicity — flat files are trivial to snapshot, rsync, or restore independently of the SQLite journal's backup cadence, providing a second, structurally simple recovery path. (4) Audit trail — since dual-write never stops (per step 3's bake period, and optionally permanently), the filesystem remains a live, independently-inspectable record that can be diffed against SQLite to catch silent corruption or divergence in the primary store. After the transition is fully validated, the file write path changes from 'primary store' to 'export': SQLite becomes the single source of truth for reads and the transactional writer, and the file write is demoted to an asynchronous, best-effort export triggered after the SQLite write commits — preserving the human-readable copy without keeping the filesystem in the critical write path or reintroducing dual-source-of-truth ambiguity long-term."}]}
</content>
